newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH INTEREST RATES SEEN ON HOLD AFTER JAN CPI.
newsitem.headline: POLISH INTEREST RATES SEEN ON HOLD AFTER JAN CPI.

text.p: The National Bank of Poland (NBP) is expected to hold official interest rates unchanged in the near-term despite slightly higher than expected January price growth, analysts said on Monday.

The Central Statistical Office (GUS) said earlier today that prices grew 2.9 percent in January, against market expectations at 2.3 percent, but the year-on-year index still fell to 18.1 percent from 18.5 percent last December.
"January price growth is roughly in line with expectations and the NBP should not move rate levels following the data," said Krzysztof Rybinski, chief economist at ING Bank in Warsaw.
Analysts said the next central bank interest rate move could be a slight reduction of rates when year-on-year inflation slides below 18 percent for good, perhaps in May.

They said that January's inflation was mainly fueled by a 7.6 percent rise in prices of services, the largest one-month jump in six years, after the government raised utility prices by 10-18 percent from the start of 1997.
"Energy price growth propelled inflation in January and the central bank may remain passive and observe interest rates for some time," said Pawel Krawczykiewicz, analyst at PBI SA bank.

Analysts said that despite the fast growth of services and a recent freeing of fuel prices, consumer price growth should slow to under two percent in February and wind-down further to around one percent per month after the first quarter.
According to a Reuter poll of leading banks in Poland inflation was forecast at 1.7 percent this month.

The central bank, which had earlier said that it would monitor broad money and price growth in January before making any decisions on official interest rates, now at 25 and 22 percent, was not immidiately available for comment.
In January, broad money rose 0.1 percent against a 6.2 percent rise in December, but analysts said changes in methods of money supply calculation made evaluation difficult.

"Because the central bank changed the way it calculates broad money, the effects of January's modest growth are not yet clear," said Tadeusz Chroscicki, chief analyst at the government's Centre for Strategic Studies (CSS).

Analysts said the troublesome growth of credit action to non-financials, whose excessive rise caused the central bank to up obligatory reserves, continued in January but that it would likely slow in months to come.
They said consumer automobile credit would likely decline in the next months as the 1997 duty-free cars imports quota would gradually dry up.
"Credit action remains high largely because of duty-free car imports, but such credit will decline in months to come as the quotas run out," CSS's Chroscicki said.
Analysts said January's 3.8 percent growth in household savings showed that propensity to save had remained intact and that the economy was not overheating, as the central bank had earlier indicated.
